p: Oh, absolutely. Yup, uh Rangers is 50 positions. Our stump removal is $2 million. It’s just OTPS. Green Thumb is 11 positions plus a little OTPS funding. We have maintenance park workers 73 positions. This is mostly CPW’s and APSW’s and some gardeners. Uh, and then 100 PEP Officers.
By chance did you list the Urban Park Rangers? Did I miss that?
The Park Rangers is 50.
50, thank you. What’s the breakdown of the Park Rangers by borough?

That’s a great question. So, let me - let me just say so overall, we have our Park Rangers are budgeted for 94 inclusive of our 50 additional - inclusive of the 50 one shot positions. I’ll look to our Deputy Commissioner Margaret Nelson

to give us a little bit more of a breakdown of how we deploy them. Uhm, but a very high level just because members may not be aware. Our Park Rangers are essentially have the same civil service title as our PEP officers, but really focus on that educational programming. So, they are the ones who you see typically running out of our nature centers, doing nature walks, doing educational programming in our public schools, providing kind of that kind of essential programming throughout our parks. They don’t typically - they don’t typically stay out of one center but are really kind of there. You’ll see rangers kind of throughout our park system at different times of the year doing really incredible educational programming. I’ll look to our Deputy Commissioner to talk a little bit more about the deployment of those Rangers.

I just want to mention you know, just for the record as well, that one third of our PEP Officers are funded by the city and if the Council didn’t fight for them, that funding wouldn’t

be there. So, I just want to just you know, say that for the record as well.

And thank you for that. So, I’m actually and I’m happy to talk to you about PEP. So, our Rangers, we do look at as a little differently than our PEP officers. They have the same civil service title but whereas our PEP Officers, you will see typically enforcing our park rules, educating the public in terms of just kind of again those park rules. They try to hit as many parks and like spaces as possible. Our rangers are doing a little bit more of like deeper programming. So, they are doing it for Black history month. We are doing a lot of history, like programming around city’s - Black leaders in the city and their impacts on parks. Rangers will do nature walks. They’ll do a little bit more of that kind of deeper - they’ll do shoreline kind of educational programming. So, a little different in terms of their overall scope. I’ll look to our Deputy Commissioner Margaret Nelson to talk a little bit more about how we deploy those rangers and I’m also happy to talk about PEP.
Thank you. Before you answer, I believe you have to be sworn in. Is that right?

Thank you Chair. Please raise your right hand if you’re able. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this Committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? Thank you.
I do.
Thank you.

As the Commissioner said, first of all, we’re incredibly grateful for the one shot funding for the Rangers. Our baseline Ranger number is only in the 40’s. And so, when you think about adding 50 more Rangers, we really have been able to expand the breadth of our programming throughout the city and we did take a special look at making sure that we are providing programming at every single Council district, which is something we weren’t able to do with our baseline staffing. So, I just want to point that out. As the Commissioner said, you know we have 11 nature centers, which are open on the weekends and we

provide programming and open hours there. We also provide programming in schools through our natural classroom program, so we’re going out into schools doing programming there and also bringing those school children into our parks. We do pop up programming and we do scheduled programming. So, it’s really throughout the city and it’s not necessarily based on you know specific parks at a specific time. So, happy to provide you more detail and I would say that those Rangers are really spread equitably across the five boroughs.
What does a typical day for a Park Ranger look like?

So, a typical day for a Park Ranger, you know they’re going to spend some of their time planning programming that is upcoming. So, they do some reaching out to schools to see if schools are interested in programming or following up on inquiries that they’ve gotten. They do - do some patrol in parks and they use that as an opportunity if they see wildlife in a park, they might gather people around and do some education. That’s called our popup programming. So, if they see a seal you know in the river or they see a hawk in a tree,

they’ll be doing pop up programming with the people that are in the park. They will also do some patrol around K9 conditions, so dogs off leash. They will try to educate folks around that. Again, as the Commissioner said, both our rangers and our PEP Officers both have the same underlying urban park ranger civil service title. They’re both trained as peace officers. They both have the ability to make arrests if needed but again, with our rangers and our PEP Officers really look for education first to educate park workers before having to move to enforcement if they do.
In the instance that they have to make an arrest, uh, the person that they have detained, will they be moved to a local precinct? Is that correct?
Exactly.
Okay, uhm, would the agency be supportive of the Council’s push for the Administration to baseline?

I think that is again, as the leader of this agency, we’d always be happy to see more certainty and more uhm and more funding in our budget. Certainly, for our rangers and for our PEP

Officers in particular, we do this - those positions take a lot of training and require a specific type of recruitment. The training alone takes around 16 weeks to do and then recruitment can take any number of weeks to do. So, I think operationally it is nice for our other kind of baseline funded positions to have that certainty in effect so that we can kind of continue and just kind of get them trained and get them out in the field as long as they’ll stay with us.

I thank you for your support. Uhm, so before I turn it over to my colleagues, I want to acknowledge Council Member Mercedes Narcisse has joined us as well. Uh, and Finance Chair Council Member Linda Lee. Uhm, I have one last uh, maybe three questions. In the Fiscal 2025 Adopted Budget there was a mix up between the Administration and the Council on funding for forestry and natural areas. This resulted in the reduction of headcount and for several people to find new employment either within or outside of the agency. The Natural Resources group is responsible for almost 1,000 acres of natural areas and performs tasks related to mulching,

watering and managing invasive species. This loss of funding will certainly lead to reductions in services that are provided by the agency and may even result in damage to our natural areas due to neglect. Can you please give a full timeline from the perspective of DPR on how this funding was lost? And then I’ll have a follow up to that.

Sure, uhm, so I - I think, again, while just to give a high level kind of overview and then I’ll look to my team to kind of speak to a little bit with more detail. But again, these one shots, uhm, these one shot funding opportunities as I understand it are really - come out of negotiations directly between the Council and the Administration. We are incredibly grateful for these opportunities and frankly a lot of times, after a couple of years of seeing these one shots coming in, it gives us a lot of uh, it gives me a lot of kind of direction and data so that I may be able to demonstrate that, maybe something shouldn’t be one shotted and it should be baselined. A good example of this is that we had gardeners that were uh, one shot - on one shot funding for several years and then uh, from what I understand the

Council and Administration kind of saw that this was something that was constantly discussed and ultimately became baselined. So, I will say that it is pretty routine and pretty typical to see these one shots come up but they are in direct communication between the Council and the Administration on how and what would ever kind of finally comes up. And so, I’ll look to you Matt to give us a little bit more detail.

Sure, thank you Commissioner. My name is Matt Drury, I’m the Chief of Citywide Legislative Affairs. Uhm, yeah, and I can kind of talk a little bit about the sort of tick tock that sort of led to the situation you described. I’ll take a step back and note that the forest management framework uh, it’s a partnership between our agency and the Natural Areas Conservancy and that was released in 2018. And what that sketched out is sort of a forward looking 25 year plan. Again, specifically looking at our forested natural areas. So, this is different and separate and apart from all of our efforts related to street trees or trees within landscape parks. So, it is very much focusing on those natural forests and uh, because obviously

natural forest health is where the vast majority of our raw- you know in terms of the raw value of individual trees that make up our canopy, our natural forests are a huge, huge part of that. So, starting in FY20, the agency received one shot expense funding. I believe that was $4.5 million. I believe there was then a pause during the COVID related FY21 discussions. That funding was resumed in FY22. In FY23 and FY24, we saw funding, one shot funding of $2.5 million. And then, and again, and so, through these years, you can think of sort of the forest management framework, staff and that sort of planning and other analysis and other work kind of getting underway, right? In FY25 for you know again, we weren’t directly involved in these discussions so it’s a little hard to speak to but it does appear that both Council and the Administration that in FY, it was not funded. However, so there were -
I guess and not to cut you off. What was the result of the loss of funding? What was the impact of it?

Yeah, there you go. For sure. So, there were 27 FMF focused staff that were employed at

the time of FY25 Adoption. 20 of those were able to stay on hand and shifted to just other grant funded parks opportunities and positions. So, 20 out of the 27 stayed onboard. Three were able to fill full-time vacancies that already existed and then four resigned and went on to other. So, 23 out of the 27 stayed on with the agency and I believe to a large degree still do today.
What’s the current budgeted and actual headcount in the forestry division?
In the forestry division; sorry, I don’t mean to split hairs but so do you mean sort of the Natural Resource Group maybe? Like, that’s sort of or do you mean forestry?
Forestry.
Uh -
So, we have uh, for forestry, we have 200 active staff who are dedicated to caring for our street and landscape park trees and that includes 58 foresters and 90 climber and pruners.
Is that enough to manage the city’s natural areas?

So, our forestry staff here actually take care of our street and it’s just a terminology thing but for our forestry staff, that’s just a team that’s taking care of our street trees and like park trees. Park trees in any given park. That’s that team. In terms of our natural areas, natural area staff, that’s our kind of - oh, I’m sorry, there are 73 in our - uh who are taking care of our natural areas space. That’s like the kind of wild more uhm, forgive me, I keep saying the word natural but more like typical forest of what you think of.
Is it enough?

I mean, we are happy to - we’re happy- I mean I think that you can look at our MMR data for how we’re doing with the resources that we have. We are again, I’m more is always more in the sense that we’re always happy to receive more resources but at the same time, I would also say that Parks has a - we understand at a very intimate level that we have mandates to uphold and essential services to provide New Yorkers, be it in our landscape parks or in our natural areas. And so,

we’re going to uphold those mandates with any resources that we’re given.
I’m having a slight challenge Commissioner. It’s not with you but you did mention something that park workers and the work that parks does is essential.
Hmm, mmm.

Uhm, but unfortunately, the way that the current budget looks, the preliminary budget looks, it doesn’t seem as if it is essential to the Administration as it stands. And so, uhm I want to just go back to a question I asked in the last hearing regarding the snow storm.
Yeah.

And regarding the staff that were required to work during the snow storm. Will the department be willing to use funds from accruals given that accruals from the current vacancy rate are projected to provide more than enough funding, to provide retroactive pay comparable to the pay provided by DSNY to those DPR staff who worked to shovel during the last snow storm?

I’m sorry, I think I just want to make sure I understand your question. So, those

staff who responded to the snow storm and happy to give you kind of again, the large overview. When we- when we have major snow events like the two that we had in just - in February, our entire maintenance and operation crew responds to those storms. Nothing else kind of takes higher priority than ensuring that we are doing our part to help New Yorkers get to where they need to go. So, that does and we have a kind of very thoughtful, very thorough, extremely dense winter weather response plan that really prioritizes perimeter sidewalks, uhm, high traffic areas, major transit hubs, kind of high part JOP’s are up there at the top. We work with our brothers and sisters at DSNY to help clear bus stations and crosswalks and really understand this to be a full city effort to get out of a storm and recover as quickly as possible. Knowing that there are priorities to helping people get around. That work, Parks works very closely in hand and hand with our other sister agencies, DSNY and NYSEM, DOT, NYPD, and FDNY to kind of respond to the storm and during while those parkies are responding, they are getting paid for

that work. So, they are there, so they are getting paid.

So, I don’t think the question has to do with them being paid. We know they were paid but it doesn’t seem that the pay was comparable to those in the Department of Sanitation and those that were hired per diem by the city. I personally feel that it’s only fair to provide equal pay for equal work, especially since some park staff had to sleep in rec centers overnight. You know that is a - that’s a huge ask and it speaks to the essential nature, I believe, of Park workers, Parkies in general. And so, I just want to - I would like to know if the agency would consider matching that pay to that of those that work the storm, that were DSNY and/or the per diem workers.

Yeah thank you. You know just one kind of caveat to that and I’d say that you know we’re happy to - I’m always happy to uplift the work of parkies. We’d have to, I think, look closer and I don’t know if I can speak to exactly how those DSNY or DOT staffers were compensated, like to do a comparison between them. Although we did provide overtime for when parkies were there.

The only caveat is that we, you know, talk a little bit about that snow storm, which was so intense. Uhm, you know, frankly only in rare occasions did we request those park staff to stay overnight. Uhm, we offered it though because we do want to take care of our staff and oftentimes, we know how important it is that the work they do, that they would go through extraordinary lengths to show up for work the next day. So, this was, oftentimes we were doing - we were kind of helping them accommodate and stay overnight in park houses and rec centers and things like that because we knew that it was going to be dangerous for them to kind of travel back and forth and that was an offer to them. Not necessarily a, uhm, you have to do this sort of thing. But uhm, just that was a small caveat.
Out of curiosity, uh, were meals provided to them for those who stayed overnight?

You know, I would have to check but in most cases, I, myself, was going around to the centers and to checking on staff during the entirety of the storm. Park staff were overall in really good spirits. They were very happy about the

situation. Most of them had all- had gotten pizza or gotten other kinds of uhm, like the managers had gotten pizza for them and kind of helped support them. In some of the rec centers, they were watching movies into the night and then like getting up the next morning doing their, and getting back to work. So, I think overall, we’re happy to give you a little bit more - look into that further but overall, we do what we can to make sure that they’re supported and most of all safe.

I’d appreciate you following back up with us. I don’t want to take too much time. I have a lot of colleagues who are here who have questions. I want to acknowledge Council Member Pierina Sanchez who has joined us as well. Uh, for questions, we’ll start in Harlem with Council Member Yusef Salaam.
Thank you Chair. Thank you for your testimony as well.
Thank you.

I want to start with Central Parks maintenance decline. It was noted there was a decrease of about $18.87 million from

Fiscal Year ‘26 to ‘27. Let us know what services or maintenance activities will be reduced and does this decline affect park cleanliness, safety or recreational programming?

Thanks for the question, Council Member. I, to my knowledge, although I’ll look to my team to see. I don’t believe that we actually have a decline of $18 million to central park. Uhm, although we can double check that to confirm. I am happy to actually talk about - there is maybe, you may have seen, there is a line in our budget that goes towards main- like funding that goes directly towards CPC’s maintenance and that is around, I think it’s $14 million, although we can confirm and I can talk a little bit about that because it is a little bit of a strange thing to see overall in our budget. But essentially this came out of uh, this comes out of our license agreement with the Central Park Conservancy. The overall maintenance of Central Park just given the kind of prominence, the landscape, the kind of long time - the long scale vision of this park is well into what I understand to be like $100 million a year, if not more. And so, that sort of

kind of matching from the city came out of their license agreement that the city struck with the Central Park Conservancy many, many years ago. And so, while the city does contribute I think, I think it’s $14 million. $16 million, $16 million uhm that is kind of matched many times over by the Central Park Conservancy. And to my knowledge that has not changed. There’s nothing in the next budget that I think is going to impact that. I do want to point out that out of the relationship also has come something I think that spans beyond Central Park, which is very important to me. CPC has and I’m sorry, I say CPC but Central Park Conservancy has agreed to partner with Parks to expand the horticulture practices and kind of maintenance of that park and expand it to other parks throughout the city. And that’s through a kind of year - an annual kind of parks, like beyond like an annual kind of parks, like beyond an annual kind of fellowship where CPC puts their resources in other parks around the city to help kind of maintain and other kind of portions of different parks. And help teach our staff and others kind of some of those practices.

We’re happy to talk a little bit more about that and I’d look to our Acting First Deputy Commissioner, if he wants to speak more to that sort of program. But in fact, our kind of relationship goes beyond just Central Park and you should see actually, we had - we were in uhm, your district in Marcus Garvey Park for awhile and then we are now I think finishing up, we finished up two years in what is it? Hybridge and then are now moving to a different park entirely but you see this kind of residency happen with CPC staff and generally we see a lot of benefits from that.

Thank you. The budget- the program budget decreased by ‘26 $75 million from Fiscal Year ‘26 to ‘27. What capital projects are being deferred or delayed and how will this impact the East River Esplanade phase three and the Halfen park pool with construction timelines?

Thank you again for the question. So, I will look through- so, I’m happy to talk through those two projects in particular. Although we’re happy to also get you more specific details. But uhm, so sorry - Okay, okay, so I’m not sure about any sort of - about the budget reduction component to what that

number is referring to. Although we can look into it and get back to you, if there is. Our kind of ten year capital plan is reflective of $12 billion of capital projects. I can talk to you a little bit specifically. We have 500 capital projects that are currently either in design, in procurement, in construction. And then we have 91 projects that are coming up in this next year. 91 projects that are kind of in the queue that have not yet started design. Uhm, and so, the two projects in particular though, I’m not aware of any sort of like outright delays for East River Esplanade. It’s one that’s very close and near and dear to my heart. Those two, like we are kind of continuing. You should see actually construction happening right now on portions of the Esplanade, particularly in East Harlem where work is happening right now and I think we just broke- did groundbreaking with you just in the last year with the kind of Harlem component to it right at 135th Street with the Halfen project. We are moving right along with this and are eager to see that rec center back and reopened.
Thank you Chair. I just have some more. Uhm, recreation membership growth versus funding. The recreation center membership increased 5.3 percent.
Hmm, mmm.

7,737 members, new members I would say in the first four months of Fiscal Year ‘26, driven by young adult growth. Does the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget include the increased funding to support expanding programming and staffing for this growing membership base.

Thank you for the question. I too am looking at membership and rec center visitation very closely. You know the truth is is that we have over a billion. $1 billion going into recreation facilities over the next several years. We opened up Shirley Chisholm this year. This won’t even be the end of the conversation around rec centers that we’re opening. We’ll be opening up Mary Cali Dalton, I hope by the end of this calendar year. We’ve got four more rec centers kind of in the queue, particularly in the Bronx, in Queens. Really exciting projects and typically when we do open up these new facilities, particularly what you saw with

Shirley, uhm we do receive additional funding to staff those facilities. The budget that you have in front of you does not reflect any additional staffing at this point, although we are kind of constantly in conversation with OMB as we open up those new centers. I will say though and as proud as I am around this major investment and opening up of new rec centers, the first in a decade. Truly is that the rec center component is just one piece of a larger puzzle of how we serve New York City in terms of our recreational programming. Outside of our rec centers, we have playground associates. We have shape up classes. We have other kind of rec programming that helps get New Yorkers access to these incredible services even if you don’t live near a rec center. So, we’re very excited and can provide you additional information around that type of network but really you should look at our rec centers as just one component and then see this larger kind of mosaic of services that we provide, even without a stationary building attached to it.

Finally, DPR received $1.6 million in state funding for lifeguard

recruitment bonuses to achieve 1,200 lifeguards. Is this efficient to meet the workforce needs for full pool and beach season? And what is the current lifeguard vacancy rate and how does this compare to Fiscal Year ‘25?

Thank you for the question, very much so. So, I just want to say in recognition of my predecessors, particularly Iris Rodriguez Rosa but also Sue Donahue, both of these Commissioners really saw what was a nationwide issue with lifeguarding and focused in- on changing the narrative in New York City. It was truly, anywhere in the country, you would see lifeguards coming in in short supply and particularly Iris, really took on the challenge of changing this around and working very closely with our union and with our lifeguards to both change how they were received within the agency but also deliver on some real kind of financial incentives to increase our numbers. So, now lifeguards are making $22 an hour. That was an increase. They also receive a $1,000 retention bonus and those two things mixed with also just a cultural shift and I wish I could spend an hour talking about this within our agency, has really resulted in

increasing numbers instead of the kind of continuously decreasing amount. And I really want to just again say thank you to Iris and Sue, who really took this on. And frankly we’re going to continue that under my leadership here. We’ve seen significant retention with this, to the tune of around 70 to 80 percent of lifeguards are now returning back. That’s higher than the national average and we had just shy of 1,100 last year's lifeguards. We had 1,082. It’s still too early to be able to tell you exactly what we’re going to have this year but I am very hopeful and the numbers are looking good. We’re just in training right now, so it kind of depends on who sticks out through training and ultimately we do the last tests and we won’t be able to know for sure until frankly the end of June, start of July in terms of our total numbers but you do feel a difference here. I have to tell you particularly even at our pools you saw, at our big olympic size pools, just a couple years ago, we were only able to open up those pools. It’s like 15 percent. It was really tight. Uhm, you know this year and this last summer, just in this last past summer, you saw diving pools opening

up. You saw we were able to bring back adult swim. Senior splash, which was such a beloved program. And so, we’re really hoping to see kind of that continued growth. And are very grateful frankly to my predecessors for their kind of - their focused effort here.
Thank you Commissioner. Thank you Chair.
Absolutely. I also want to give kudos to the formal Commissioner Iris Rodriguez Rosa. She did amazing work, so I just want to - I know she’s watching so-
Yeah, I know. She’ll be testing, yes.
I want to - let’s travel to Queens. Uh, to my neighbor Council Member Lynn Schulman.

Thank you Chair and I want to Commissioner, welcome and uhm, I did this privately. I’ll say it publicly. I think you’re going to be a great Commissioner and I know you from a lot of other things plus you’re the Manhattan right, Commissioner. So, you have a wealth of knowledge and all of that and you’ve been

particularly helpful to me recently, so anyway uhm, we look forward to your great work. I have a few questions. One is about accessibility. So, I have actually funded accessible access to Forest Park and then I’m told that it’s going to take years for anything to happen because you don’t have enough engineers. So that’s one. Uhm, and this is - you know this is a fully funded project that we - you know that I did in my first year so, that’s - so that’s the first question.

Yup, thank you first and most importantly for your partnership and for your continued advocacy for our parks. I very much appreciate it. Uhm, second of all, thank you also for prioritizing accessibility in your parks. Uhm, I truly think at a very high level, we should be judged based on how we serve our most vulnerable and that means our accessibility. So, I appreciate the funding and the continued follow up here. You know while I’m happy to give you a specific update as to where we stand on this. It is true that that these projects are capital projects and it doesn’t really matter if we’re talking about a bathroom but in this case, we’re talking about

accessibility, accessible pathways into our parks. They do take quite a long time. And truly uhm, I can go into details around this but the truth of the matter is, is that we are looking at very closely at how we can shave down some of this time. Really what you see is when you start design, design may be and it’s been pretty typical around 12-ish months.
I haven’t even seen a design yet. So, we’re told that you know there’s not enough personnel to do that.

Hmm, hmm, when you see those design, those design parks when it gets into design, uhm, but for any project or a project that’s right before your project or where our uhm, after the design phase you really do see and what we’re looking at very closely is a kind of prolonged time when we’re trying to get through some regulations and kind of checks with our other agencies. All good things, truly good things but things like and you may hear this word a lot, the swhip process or something else like that. Those kind of - those types of checks within our other agencies are very important but also a time just can really lengthen projects significantly. We’re looking at

this closely, there are some things that the agency has done, actually a piece of legislation that Council Member Krishnan had passed just a few years ago around the whole capital process and ways to actually shorten this. I read, I both read your legislation and the report that came out, which was very helpful and the agency has taken steps to actually reduce some of this. We need to be doing more. So, we will certainly get back to you on this one.

Because it’s a park that’s accessed by everyone including the Chairs, constituents and you know it’s rather big, so. Alright, that’s one. The other is what is the new process now for trees to get trees planted because a lot of the public doesn’t know about that or there’s issues and so -

Yeah, thank you for the question. So, in recognizing that every single community in New York City deserves trees. Every single community needs to benefit from the overall canopy. We, the agency, has shifted away from what was a very long kind of adhoc list of 311’s and elected official requests, kind of where we were

jumping around to different areas based on the requests that came in and then decided to shift to a comprehensive tree planting plan. The good news is with this plan that I can tell you that in nine years, which is I know a long time but in nine years time, I can confidently say to you that every single corner of this city will have been reviewed, assessed and planted for but not only are we planting but we’re also expanding tree pits for overall tree health, we’re removing stumps. We’re filling empty tree pits that can no longer sustain trees in them and really touching every single corner. So, typically it is from essentially in this - in these nine years, we will be able to touch every single corner of the city. For specifically for your exact neighborhood or if you have a specific location, we’re happy to look that up and tell you where we are in the queue because you know -
It’s done through the Parks Department now?
It’s done through the Parks Department, yes.
And can you explain art work in the parks and you know that -
Yes.
Because a lot of people don’t realize and I figured that out, so -

I love art work in the parks frankly. Just to be very clear, we have a really great program where for 364 days you can work with our agency to put up art work in our parks and we know that this is not just a luxury. This is something that shows investment. It shows excitement. It can show a sense of place and pride of place as in the case of the one that you and I were just working with in Queens and so, we are very excited to work with artists of all types to really think through how they might be able to showcase their art in parks and I actually think there are some advocates here today who have run really successful sculptural programs, photography programs, who are showcasing their work in the parks. They should work with us. We’re excited about the opportunities here and if you have a park space or a green street or some other space that you think could

be activated by art work, we would love to hear about it.
But do you mind if I just finish up my - so, just so folks understand, it’s for a year? Like there’s - it’s under the Charter? That’s what I want people to know.

Yes, it is. So, we base our rules off of the Public Design Committee, which is also based on the Charter. If you do something, if you hold a piece of art work for over a year or at a year, then it requires additional kind of reviews. It is then seen as a permanent art work but we like to have - we are committed to having temporary art work that can have a revolving kind of audience and have other opportunities to bring in other artists, so in order not to trigger some other uhm, other kind of problems with adherence to the Charter and around kind of permanent art work, we do it for 364 days.

Okay and then my last question is who has because we get a lot of constituent complaints about the sidewalks when they’re lifted up by the tree roots. Like who has responsibility for that because we can’t seem to get answers to that in general.

Well, first of all, I’m very sorry because I understand how frustrating this is for very human people focused agencies. So, I don’t want any of your constituents or anyone in the city frankly to not feel like they’re getting a direct answer from parks and so, we are happy to follow up directly with you and your constituents but it typically is the property owners responsibility. However, there are some situations, we do have a program for single family homes where parks can help take care of some of that work. We still want to know about it so that we can monitor these things, so it’s probably worth a larger conversation but would love to follow up directly with your team.
Thank you for the accommodation.
